title: Festival platform: Azure or AWS
subtitle: One decision on what the Acme Tickets platform should run on, mapped to each cloud, with the monthly cost side by side.

verdict.text: Run the 6 services as serverless containers with one zone-redundant managed database and private data stores in one EU region, and put that on AWS (ECS on Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL, `eu-central-1`) at 1,998.27 USD a month, against 3,495.93 USD for the same design on Azure, at list prices from the saved tables of 2026-11-10, with ECR storage on the AWS side not priced. The binding constraint on the design is who can run it, with 6 services one too many for a managed app platform and 1 platform engineer one short of Kubernetes, and the cloud is then decided by cost and by the ECS and PostgreSQL already running in this estate.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.intro: The brief leaves these open and the request was to assume rather than ask. Each one sits next to the decision it drives.

items: **The team is the one that runs this estate [guess].** The brief does not say which company the 8 engineers come from. This repository shows ECS and PostgreSQL 17.6 in production (`infra/terraform/app.tf:31`, `infra/terraform/data.tf:12-13`). **Drives:** the choice of cloud, on what the team has to learn.

**Regions: `eu-central-1` and West Europe.** The README names `eu-central-1` for production. The saved Azure table prices only West Europe, a different EU location, so prices are close but not for the same place. Both have availability zones [med]. **Drives:** every price, and EU residency on both clouds.

**The database engine differs by cloud.** AWS is priced as RDS PostgreSQL, as the estate runs. The saved Azure table holds Azure SQL and no PostgreSQL Flexible Server, so Azure is priced on Azure SQL. **Drives:** the largest line on each bill, and an engine change if Azure were chosen.

**8 vCPU is a starting size on both clouds [guess].** db.m6i.2xlarge against 8 vCore Gen5. Nothing in the brief says how many queries a request makes. **Drives:** 1,238.08 USD on AWS and 1,564.54 USD on Azure, which the load test may change.
**Queues and secrets count as data stores,** because messages carry customer data [guess]. **Drives:** Service Bus Premium on Azure, and interface endpoints for SQS and Secrets Manager on AWS.

**S3 goes through an interface endpoint, not the free gateway endpoint.** The brief says private addresses, and only an interface endpoint gives S3 one [med]. **Drives:** 17.52 USD a month on AWS, which a gateway endpoint would save if a route and a bucket policy are accepted as private.

**Compute, the same on both clouds:** 6 services × 2 replicas or tasks × 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB, all month [guess]. Azure is billed entirely at the active rate, the conservative reading. **Drives:** the compute lines.

**A drop:** one in the priced month, 40 extra replicas or tasks for one hour, 0.72 M requests, 24 load balancer capacity units for that hour [guess]. **Drives:** a few USD of compute. The drop moves the database size, not the compute bill.

**Volumes, the same on both clouds:** 10 requests a second steady, 1,500 GB out, 2 TB between compute and data, 60 GB of logs, 1 M secret calls, 500 GB of exports [guess]. On AWS, 200 GB of the 2 TB goes through endpoints, and 1,000 GB crosses a zone, the rest stays in zone. **Drives:** several small lines.

**Outbound internet is needed on AWS** for an external email provider and logs, so two NAT gateways are priced [guess]. **Drives:** the outbound path line on AWS. Azure environments reach the internet without a separate NAT line [med].
**Six services are 1 web, 4 internal and 1 worker [guess].** The brief gives only the total. **Drives:** which service is public.

**Background work is not event-driven,** because the brief says work arrives as web requests. A few seconds is taken as 0.1 minutes. **Drives:** functions out, which the container rule decides anyway.
**One network,** with no other team or system to peer with. The brief names none. **Drives:** hub and spoke out.

**The new Container Apps environment rows apply to the Consumption plan [med].** They took effect on 2026-11-01. **Drives:** 73.00 USD a month on Azure. **Registry:** Premium on Azure so that a surviving zone can still pull images [med], 50.66 USD a month.

blocks.text:
**The binding constraint on the design is who can run it.** One platform engineer rules out Kubernetes, and 6 services is one more than a managed app platform holds, so that margin is thin. Serverless containers are all that is left on the compute ladder, on either cloud. The neutral design is the same on both: only the services change.

**The cloud is decided by what the team has to learn and by cost.** Both clouds pass the first question: nobody patches anything on either one. AWS needs more parts to be wired by hand, an ALB, NAT per zone, endpoints and policies, where Container Apps has ingress and scale rules built in [med]. Against that, this repository already runs ECS and RDS PostgreSQL, so AWS asks for no new platform and no engine change, if the team is the one that runs this estate. Then cost: AWS is 1,497.66 USD a month less, 42.8% below Azure.

**The gap does not depend on one guess.** Service Bus Premium is 677.08 USD against 2.52 USD for SQS, and Azure compute is 753.40 USD against 249.82 USD. Even with every Azure vCPU at the idle rate (saving 473.04 USD) and Service Bus Premium removed altogether (saving 677.08 USD, before the cost of Storage queues, which the saved table does not price), Azure would be 2,345.81 USD, still 347.54 USD above AWS.

**Where AWS meets the privacy rule by policy.** RDS has only private addresses. S3, SQS and Secrets Manager are regional APIs with no "public access off" switch [med]: the interface endpoints give them private addresses, and a resource policy must deny every request that does not come through the endpoint, so the public name still answers, with a refusal [med]. Azure closes these at the network with public access off. This passes the brief, but only if those policies are written and tested: see the acceptance criteria.

**On Azure the queue is the costly limit.** Service Bus Standard has no private endpoint [high], so at 10.00 USD a month it fails the brief. Storage queues on a private endpoint would pass, and the saved table has no row to price them.

All prices come from the saved tables as of 2026-11-10, at list price before tax.

blocks.text: **Not priced: ECR image storage on AWS.** The saved table has no ECR row and the request was not to go online, so the AWS total leaves it out. It is billed by storage for a few images and is small [med], but the total of 1,998.27 USD is slightly understated. **The AWS free allowances are also left out:** the free tier rows are not in the data transfer row, so outbound data is priced in full. **Left out on both clouds as too small or not in the tables:** object and blob operations, DNS, certificates, KMS and backup storage beyond the free retention.

**Costed choices that do not change the answer.** Arm images on Fargate would save 49.70 USD a month if the 6 images are built for it. Pulling images through ECR interface endpoints instead of NAT would add 35.04 USD and save 8.40 USD of data at 200 GB, so NAT stays. A dedicated Azure workload profile is not cheaper at this size [med].

items: **The team knows Azure and not ECS, or wants one fewer engine change:** Azure becomes worth paying for only if the 1,497.66 USD a month (17,971.92 USD a year) buys less than the cost of learning ECS. On the neutral design nothing else moves.
**PostgreSQL must stay and Azure is wanted:** price Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, which the saved table does not hold, before deciding.

**Someone names a WAF or bot protection, likely for a public ticket drop:** the network climbs one rung. On AWS it adds 26.20 USD a month with a WAF on the ALB (5 rules assumed, managed rule groups may cost more [med]). On Azure it adds 397.85 USD for an Application Gateway.

**The load test shows the database short at 8 vCPU:** db.m6i.4xlarge on AWS at 3,236.35 USD a month still fits the budget. On Azure, 14 vCores is the most the budget allows. Sustained traffic of 1,000 requests a second or more reopens read replicas.

**The 6 services become 5 or fewer:** a managed app platform reopens. **Two or more platform engineers together with a real need for the Kubernetes API or 15 services:** Kubernetes reopens. **A region loss stops being accepted:** two regions, a tested failover and about double the bill, which goes past the budget on Azure.

blocks.code:
# ADR-001: Run the festival platform on ECS Fargate in eu-central-1 with private data stores

Date: 2026-11-10
Status: Proposed

## Context
The next Acme Tickets platform serves three festivals a year. A ticket drop peaks at about
600 requests a second for about 20 minutes; the rest of the year load is steady and small.
Six services already ship as container images, run by 8 engineers, 1 of them a platform
engineer. About 400 GB of relational data and exported files must stay in the EU and be
reachable only on private addresses, and only the web tier may face the internet. The
system must survive the loss of one availability zone; a region loss is accepted. The
budget is at most 5,000 USD a month. The same design is estimated at 1,998.27 USD a month
on AWS (ECR storage not priced) and 3,495.93 USD on Azure, at list prices from the saved
tables of 2026-11-10. The estate already runs ECS and PostgreSQL.

## Decision
We will run the six services on ECS Fargate in eu-central-1, in private subnets of two
zones, with at least two tasks per service and one internet-facing load balancer in front
of the web tier. We will store the data in one RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance, sized at
db.m6i.2xlarge until the load test confirms it, with exports in S3, messages in SQS and
secrets in Secrets Manager, each reached through an interface endpoint and closed by a
resource policy. We will use a NAT gateway per zone for outbound traffic. We will not use
Kubernetes, read replicas or a second region.

## Consequences
Easier: nobody patches a node, one platform engineer can run this, and the estate's ECS
and PostgreSQL skills carry over.
Harder: the team writes and tests the resource policies that keep S3, SQS and Secrets
Manager private, wires scaling by hand, and must scale up before each drop.
We accept: a public web tier without a WAF until someone names that requirement, the loss
of service during a region outage, and a database size that the load test may change.

items: Which cloud do the 8 engineers already know? This is the fact most likely to change the recommendation.
Which relational engine stays? PostgreSQL on Azure needs prices the saved table does not hold.
Is 8 vCPU enough at 600 requests a second? Only a load test can say.
Is bot protection or a WAF needed for a public ticket drop? The brief does not say.
What does ECR image storage cost? It has no row in the saved table.
Is the Azure SQL IO rate meter billed on a provisioned General Purpose database? The saved table carries it (0.238 USD per 1M) and it is not on the bill.
Which email provider sends the emails, and what does it cost? It is on neither bill.
How much backup and long-term retention does the data need? Storage beyond the free retention is on neither bill.
